sections.title: Overview
sections.text: Mughal miniature painting emerged in the 16th and 17th centuries as a highly refined court art form associated with the Mughal emperors and their ateliers. These paintings were often created for manuscripts, albums, or ceremonial commissions and drew on Persian, Indian, and European influences. Their visual sophistication helped define a courtly idiom that blended learning, hierarchy, and artistic innovation.

sections.title: Production and style
sections.text: Miniature painters worked in organized workshops, where calligraphy, illustration, and courtly themes were combined under strong imperial supervision. The works often feature precise linework, jewel-like color, and carefully controlled compositions designed to communicate rank, narrative, and the idealized world of the Mughal court. Their visual language balanced realism with stylization.

sections.title: Historical significance
sections.text: The Mughal court valued painting as a record of imperial authority, ceremonial life, and literary culture. Paintings were used to document events, preserve memory, and create a visual identity for the emperor and his household. Their widespread circulation preserved a vivid record of Mughal taste and political culture.
